section.title: Rejection and the Death of John
section.sectionRationale: The tone darkens. Jesus is rejected in His own hometown, marvelling at their unbelief. He sends the Twelve out in vulnerable dependence to preach repentance. Then Mark tells, in grim flashback, how Herod murdered John the Baptist, the forerunner whose fate foreshadows the fate of the One he announced. Rejection of God's messengers is the shadow over the mission.
section.thesis: The kingdom advances through rejected and vulnerable messengers: Jesus dishonoured at home, the Twelve sent out with nothing but His authority, and John the Baptist put to death by a weak king's pride, so that the servants share their Master's path of suffering even as the word goes forward.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the rejection at Nazareth; the sending of the Twelve; and the martyrdom of John the Baptist at Herod's banquet.

units.label: The rejection at Nazareth
units.note: a prophet without honor at home

verses.text: Jesus went on from there and came to His hometown, accompanied by His disciples.

When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles?
Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” And they took {{skandalizo|offense}} at Him.
Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a {{prophetes|prophet}} without honor.”
So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them.
And He was amazed at their {{apistia|unbelief}}. And He went around from village to village, teaching the people.
Then Jesus called the Twelve to Him and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing but a staff for the journey, no bread, no bag, no money in their belts,
and to wear sandals, but not a second tunic.
And He told them, “When you enter a house, stay there until you leave that area.
If anyone will not welcome you or listen to you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.”
So they set out and preached that the people should {{metanoeo|repent}}.
They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil.

units.label: The martyrdom of John the Baptist

verses.text: Now King Herod heard about this, for Jesus’ name had become well known, and people were saying, “John the Baptist has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.”
Others were saying, “He is Elijah,” and still others, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.”
But when Herod heard this, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!”
For Herod himself had ordered that John be arrested and bound and imprisoned, on account of his brother Philip’s wife Herodias, whom Herod had married.
For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!”
So Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him. But she had been unable,
because Herod feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a {{dikaios|righteous}} and holy man. When he heard John’s words, he was greatly perplexed; yet he listened to him gladly.
On Herod’s birthday, her opportunity arose. Herod held a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee.
When the daughter of Herodias came and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests, and the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.”
And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!”
Then she went out and asked her mother, “What should I request?” And her mother answered, “The head of John the Baptist.”
At once the girl hurried back to the king with her request: “I want you to give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter immediately.”
The king was consumed with sorrow, but because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her.
So without delay, the king commanded that John’s head be brought in. He sent an executioner, who went and beheaded him in the prison.
The man brought John’s head on a platter and presented it to the girl, who gave it to her mother.
When John’s disciples heard about this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

skandalizo.gloss: To cause to stumble, to give offense, to trip up. The people of Nazareth are tripped up by Jesus' familiar origins; because they think they know Him, they refuse to reckon with the wisdom and power staring them in the face. Familiarity breeds a stumbling unbelief.

prophetes.gloss: A prophet, one who speaks God's word. Jesus places Himself in the line of the prophets who were dishonoured by their own, a line that runs through John the Baptist and reaches back through Israel's history of resisting God's messengers.

apistia.gloss: Unbelief, faithlessness. Jesus marvels at the unbelief of Nazareth, the opposite of the faith He commended in the bleeding woman and Jairus. Unbelief does not defeat His power but does close the door on receiving it, so that He does few mighty works there.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, to change one's mind and turn to God. The Twelve carry the same message Jesus and John preached: repent. The kingdom's advance calls for the turning of the whole life, and the messengers press this summons from town to town.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, just, upright. Even Herod recognized John as a righteous and holy man and feared him. Yet recognition without repentance could not save Herod from his pride; he silenced the righteous man rather than heed him, a warning about hearing truth gladly yet not obeying it.

basic.context: Jesus returns to Nazareth, and the people who watched Him grow up cannot get past the carpenter they think they know; they take offense, and He marvels at their unbelief. He then sends the Twelve out two by two with almost nothing, dependent on His authority and on the hospitality of others, to preach repentance, cast out demons, and heal. Mark then pauses to tell how John the Baptist died: how the fearless prophet rebuked Herod's unlawful marriage, how Herodias schemed, and how a rash oath at a birthday banquet led to John's beheading. The messenger who prepared the way meets a violent end.
basic.hermeneutics: This section is about the cost of the mission. Jesus is rejected at home, the Twelve are sent in vulnerability and will meet rejection too, and John is martyred. John's death, told after the sending of the Twelve, casts its shadow forward over Jesus and all His servants. The gladly-listening but disobedient Herod is a sober study in hearing without heeding.
basic.originalLanguages: Nazareth is skandalizo, tripped up, by the familiar Jesus, and He marvels at their apistia, unbelief. He is a prophetes, a prophet, without honour at home. The Twelve preach that people should metanoeo, repent. And Herod knew John was dikaios, righteous, yet killed him anyway.
basic.typology: John the Baptist is the new Elijah, and his conflict with Herod and Herodias echoes Elijah's with Ahab and Jezebel. The dishonoured prophet and the murdered forerunner both prefigure the rejection and death of Christ Himself.
basic.christ: Jesus is the prophet dishonoured by His own, walking the road every faithful messenger walks. John's fate is a preview of Jesus' own arrest and death. Even the speculation about who Jesus is, John raised, Elijah, a prophet, circles the deeper truth Mark has already told us.
basic.god: God's word goes forward through weak and rejected messengers, not through worldly power. God calls His servants to depend on Him, and He honours faithfulness even to death.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 19 and 21 set Elijah against Ahab and Jezebel. Matthew 10 parallels the sending of the Twelve. Hebrews 11 honours the prophets who suffered.
basic.oneStory: Israel's long history of rejecting God's prophets reaches into the ministry of Jesus and John. The forerunner is killed, foreshadowing the death of the One he announced. Yet the kingdom does not depend on human welcome; it advances through faithful, vulnerable, even martyred messengers, all the way to the cross where the ultimate rejected Messenger wins the world's salvation.

context.literary:
Mark 6:1-29 is built as a sandwich, and the filling is the grimmest story in the Gospel. The Twelve are sent out in 6:7-13 and return in 6:30, and between those two verses Mark inserts the account of how John the Baptist died. The arrangement does what Mark's sandwiches always do: the inner story interprets the outer. The Twelve go out with authority and a message of repentance; the reader is told in the middle of their mission what happens to those who preach repentance to the powerful. The first mission and the first martyrdom are set side by side, and neither can be read without the other.

The passage opens with a failure and a reversal. At Nazareth, 6:1-6, Jesus is rejected and can do little, and the next scene shows Him handing His own authority to the Twelve. A rejected Messiah does not retreat. He multiplies His work. Mark ends the Nazareth story with Jesus 'amazed,' and the next section moves at once to a mission that goes door to door through the villages.

The story of John is told as a flashback. It is introduced at 6:14 by what Herod hears about Jesus, and then Mark takes eleven verses to tell how John came to be dead. The scene moves in three steps: Herod's ambivalent attitude toward John in 6:17-20, the banquet and the oath in 6:21-26, and the execution and burial in 6:27-29. The weight falls on the middle, where a king is trapped by his own words in front of his guests. Mark cares less about the death itself than about the way a man who hears a prophet gladly can be made to destroy him.

There are many links back to what has gone before. The vocabulary of 'hearing' from chapter 4 is present again in Herod's gladly hearing. The words 'offense' and 'unbelief' belong with the parable of the sower. The authority over unclean spirits given to the Twelve is the authority that Jesus gave in 3:15. And the next scene, 6:30-44, sets the banquet of a king, where a man's head is carried in on a platter, against a banquet in the wilderness, where Jesus feeds a crowd with bread and fish. The two meals are meant to be read together.
context.historical:
Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee, and everyone in it knew everyone else. The people's questions in 6:2-3 are the questions of a community that had watched Jesus grow up. 'The carpenter,' tekton, was a builder who worked in wood and also in stone, which is why the word is sometimes translated 'builder.' To call Jesus 'the son of Mary' is unusual, since a man was normally identified by his father. It may be a mark of the way they were speaking of Him, or it may mean that Joseph had died, and Mark does not say. They list four brothers by name and mention sisters, in a way that shows how well they knew His family.

Honour and shame were at the heart of village life. To be taught by someone you had known as a child, and to take offence at his authority, was a village's way of defending its sense of how things should be. The proverb Jesus quotes in 6:4 was a familiar one, and Luke's account gives it with the stories of Elijah and Elisha going to outsiders, Luke 4:24-27.

The instructions for the mission in 6:8-11 fit the practice of travel in a world of hospitality. Travellers depended on being taken in. Shaking the dust from the feet was a gesture of separation, and some Jews are said to have shaken off the dust of Gentile land when returning to the Holy Land, so it was a sign that a place was being treated as outside the people of God. Sending them in pairs matched the legal principle that testimony needed two witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15, and it gave the travellers company and protection. Anointing with oil was a customary remedy as well as a religious act.

Herod is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch. Mark calls him 'king,' as the popular title for him, while Matthew and Luke give his proper rank, tetrarch, Matthew 14:1 and Luke 3:19. The Jewish historian Josephus also records that Antipas had John put to death, and he places it at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, giving a political reason, that Herod feared John's influence over the crowds. Mark and Josephus supplement each other, since Mark gives the personal reason and Josephus the political one. The marriage of Herod and Herodias broke the law of Leviticus 18:16, and John's protest, 'It is not lawful,' is an appeal to that law. A birthday banquet for 'the nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee' belonged to the world of the Roman client kings, with the sort of display and drinking in which a ruler could be pushed into a rash promise.
context.canonical:
The rejection at Nazareth belongs to a long Old Testament pattern of God's messengers dishonoured by their own. Joseph's brothers said 'Here comes that dreamer!' and plotted to kill him, Genesis 37:19-20. Israel rejected Moses with the words 'Who made you ruler and judge?' and yet God sent that same man as ruler and redeemer, as Stephen recalls in Acts 7:35. The men of Anathoth sought the life of Jeremiah, Jeremiah 11:21, and God warned him that even his brothers and his father's household had betrayed him, Jeremiah 12:6. Jesus' words about prophets honoured everywhere but at home put Him in that company.

The sending of the Twelve has its roots in the Exodus. At the first Passover Israel ate with 'your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand,' Exodus 12:11, ready to travel. The disciples are told to take a staff and wear sandals, the same equipment, and they too are set out on a journey that depends on God. Luke records that the instruction not to carry a purse was later adjusted for a new time, Luke 22:35-36, and Paul says that the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from it, 1 Corinthians 9:14. Matthew 10:5-10 and Luke 9:1-6 and 10:1-12 give parallel instructions.

John's story is bound up with Elijah. Mark has already dressed John in Elijah's clothes, a leather belt and rough clothing, Mark 1:6 and 2 Kings 1:8, and Malachi 4:5-6 promises that the LORD would send Elijah before the great day. Jesus will say that Elijah has already come and that 'they have done to him whatever they wished,' Mark 9:11-13. Herodias plays the part of Jezebel, who vowed to make Elijah's life like the lives of the prophets he had killed, 1 Kings 19:1-2. The scene at Herod's banquet also echoes Esther, where a king says to his queen 'up to half the kingdom,' Esther 5:3 and 5:6. In Esther the promise is used to save a people; in Mark it is used to destroy a prophet.

Finally, the pattern of the suffering messenger continues in the rest of Scripture. Hebrews 11:36-38 lists those who were mocked, flogged and put to the sword, of whom 'the world was not worthy.' John's death is the first of a line leading through Stephen and James to a long history of martyrs, and it points to the death of the One he announced.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wants his readers to see that following Jesus is not a path of general acceptance. The passage starts with the Lord Himself rejected by those who knew Him best. The first readers, many of them cut off from their own families and towns, would have recognised the experience. Mark's message to them is that rejection by one's own is not a sign that something has gone wrong with the mission. It happened to the Lord.

He also wants them to understand how the mission works. The Twelve go out light, with authority and a short message, and they depend on the hospitality of strangers. They are not told to succeed. They are told to go, to stay where they are welcomed, and to leave a testimony where they are not. The test is faithfulness. A church that thought it needed money and status to be effective is being told otherwise.

The story of John carries a pointed lesson. John is the model of the faithful witness who speaks truth to a ruler at the cost of his life. Herod is the model of the hearer who is drawn to the truth and never obeys it. Mark makes sure his readers see both. He also wants us to feel the shadow over the whole Gospel: the one who prepared the way for Jesus has been killed by a man who would not act on what he knew, and the same is about to happen to Jesus.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Nazareth story records a rejection and Jesus' response to it. It is not a rule that a believer should expect to be rejected by every family member or should turn away from those who do not accept the message. It is, though, a caution against assuming that familiarity and insight go together. The people who knew Jesus best were not the ones who saw Him most clearly.

The mission instructions are the hardest part of the passage to apply. They are descriptive of one particular mission, and Jesus later changes some of the terms, Luke 22:35-36. They are not a command that every missionary must go without money or a bag. What continues is the principle behind them: those who are sent depend on God and on the people they serve, they do not make their message depend on resources, and they accept that some will not receive them. We should not turn the details into a law, but we should not discard the principle either.

John's death is recorded, not commended or required. Nothing in the account tells believers to provoke rulers. It shows what faithful speech to a powerful person can cost, and Jesus Himself will affirm John's role. The story invites us to speak the truth plainly where it is needed, and to do so knowing the possible price, without suggesting that martyrdom is something to be sought. Herod's oath is also a warning, though not a command: a person who makes a promise in front of an audience can become trapped by it, and Mark shows that this is no way to rule.

debates.question: Why could Jesus do no mighty work at Nazareth?

views.label: A moral limitation, not a lack of power
views.case: Unbelief did not drain Jesus of power. Rather, in the face of settled contempt He withheld His mighty works, since His miracles were meant to meet faith, not to impress the hardened. Matthew softens Mark's 'could not' to 'did not,' Matthew 13:58, which shows how the early church read it.

views.label: Miracles answer faith
views.case: Jesus still healed a few sick people, so the point is that His mighty works answer to those who come seeking Him. Nazareth's offence closed the door on the blessing they might have received, as when others came in faith, Mark 5:34 and 10:52.

views.label: The wording shows the real difficulty of unbelief
views.case: Mark's plain 'He could not' is deliberate. It does not diminish Jesus but shows that God has chosen to work through a relationship of trust, so that where trust is absent the work is impeded. His amazement at their unbelief, in contrast with the faith He marvels at in Matthew 8:10, makes the same point.

debates.bearing: Each view guards against two errors: Jesus is not powerless before unbelief, and He is not a spectacle-worker who forces His gifts on those who despise Him. Unbelief forfeits the blessing.

debates.question: Do the mission instructions of verses 8 to 11 still bind those who are sent?

views.label: They are a standing model
views.case: Some hold that those called to full-time ministry should live simply, trusting God to provide through the hospitality of others. They cite 1 Corinthians 9:14 and the many missionaries who have gone out without a guaranteed income.

views.label: They were for that mission only
views.case: Jesus reverses part of the instruction on the eve of His death, telling them to take a purse and bag, Luke 22:35-36. Mark also allows a staff and sandals where Matthew and Luke do not, which suggests the details were not a fixed law. Paul worked with his hands at times so as not to burden others, 1 Corinthians 9:15-18.

views.label: A principle of dependence, not a rule of equipment
views.case: The point of the details is that the Twelve go in simple trust and in the Lord's authority. How that is lived varies with time and place, and the principle is that the messenger does not rely on resources or comfort. Both Paul's tentmaking and the support of churches fit that.

debates.bearing: The third view gathers what is true in the others. The aim is dependence on God and openness to the hospitality He provides, and no particular list of equipment is required.

debates.question: Which Philip was Herodias's husband, and how does Mark fit with Josephus?

views.label: A half-brother also called Philip
views.case: Mark says Herodias had been the wife of Herod's brother Philip. Josephus names her first husband as another Herod. Some propose that this son of Herod the Great bore both names, and that Philip the tetrarch of the north was a different man.

views.label: Mark's information is imprecise
views.case: Others suppose that Mark, or the tradition he used, confused the two Philips, since the Herodian family was large and its names repeated. The error would not affect the point of the story, that the marriage broke the law.

views.label: The accounts give different angles on the same event
views.case: Josephus, writing about politics, and Mark, writing about a prophet, report different parts of the same story. Differences of detail in a family tree of this kind are no reason to doubt the central event, which Josephus confirms.

debates.bearing: The family history is tangled, and we do not have to settle it. What every account agrees on is that Herod married his brother's wife, John denounced it, and John was put to death.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with verse 3, where the people 'took offense' at Him. The verb is skandalizo, from skandalon, the trigger of a trap or a stone that makes a person trip. It is the same verb that Jesus used of the shallow soil in the parable of the sower, 4:17, where those with no root 'fall away' when trouble comes. Here the village trips over the ordinary. They cannot get past the carpenter they know to the authority He carries. In Mark's use, then, the offence is not an emotional reaction but a stumbling over what is too close to be believed.

In verse 5 Mark says, 'He could not perform any miracles there,' using the verb dynamai, 'to be able,' and the word for miracle is dynamis, power. Mark has used dynamis in 5:30 of the power that went out of Jesus when the woman touched Him. The sentence puts powerless and powerful side by side. Matthew changes the wording to say that Jesus 'did not' do many mighty works, Matthew 13:58, but Mark leaves the harder word. The next sentence has Jesus 'amazed,' ethaumazen, at their unbelief, apistia. Elsewhere in the Gospels Jesus marvels at faith, as with the centurion in Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9. Here He marvels at its absence.

The word for 'prophet' in verse 4 is prophetes, and the proverb describes him as atimos, 'without honour.' The word is the opposite of timao, to honour, which links it to the fifth commandment, 'Honor your father and your mother,' Exodus 20:12, and shows the force of the saying. In the place where honour should be most natural, it is missing.

In the sending, verse 7, Jesus 'began to send them out,' apostellein, the verb behind the word 'apostle.' At 3:14 they were appointed so that He might send them, and now the sending begins. The phrase 'two by two,' dyo dyo, is a Semitic idiom of repetition. They are given authority over unclean spirits, exousia, the same word used in 3:15. The instruction to take 'nothing but a staff' uses the word rhabdos for the staff, which is the word used for the staff of Moses and of travellers, and the allowance of sandals but not a second tunic is precise.

The preaching of the Twelve is described by the verb kerysso, to proclaim as a herald, and the content is 'that people should repent,' metanoeo. This is the same call Jesus made in 1:15 and the same verb John used. The message is not new; the Twelve are carrying Jesus' own message and John's. Anointing with oil uses aleipho, the ordinary word for rubbing with oil, found again in James 5:14.

Verse 14 begins with the report of Herod, and the identification of Jesus with John uses a passive form: 'he has been raised,' egerthe, from egeiro. It is the verb for resurrection that Mark will use of Jesus at 16:6. Herod's conscience is already speaking in the language of resurrection.

In verses 17 and 18 the arrest of John is described with krateo, 'to seize,' the verb Mark used for the family's attempt to seize Jesus in 3:21 and which he will use for Jesus' arrest in 14:44. John had been 'bound' and thrown into prison. Mark's wording for John's being handed over, in 1:14, uses paradidomi, and that is the verb that will mark the passion of Jesus and the persecution of His followers.

Verse 20 describes Herod with three telling verbs. He 'feared' John, ephobeito; he 'protected' him, synetrei, a word for keeping safe; and he 'listened to him gladly,' hedeos ekouen, with an adverb that Mark uses again of the crowds who heard Jesus gladly, 12:37. The adjective 'greatly perplexed' is aporeo, to be at a loss. Herod is like the rocky ground of the parable, who hear and receive with joy and yet bear no fruit, 4:16-17. John is described with the pair dikaios kai hagios, 'righteous and holy.'

In verse 26, the king is 'consumed with sorrow,' perilypos, a word that Mark uses of only one other person. In Gethsemane Jesus says His soul is perilypos to the point of death, 14:34. The king's grief belongs to a man who will do what he is sorry for; the Lord's belongs to One who will do what He grieves to face. And the executioner in verse 27 is a speculator, a Latin loanword for a guard of the Roman type. Finally, in verse 29 the body that John's disciples take is a ptoma, a corpse, the same word Mark uses at 15:45 when Joseph of Arimathea asks for Jesus' body, and they lay it in a tomb, mnemeion, as Joseph will lay Jesus.

typology.type: The prophet rejected by his own: Joseph, Moses, Jeremiah
typology.fulfillment: Joseph's brothers mocked him as 'that dreamer,' Genesis 37:19, Israel asked Moses 'Who made you ruler and judge?' Acts 7:35, and Jeremiah was betrayed by his own family, Jeremiah 12:6. In each case God's chosen deliverer was refused by the very people he came to save, and then became their rescuer. Jesus stands in the same line at Nazareth and escalates it: He is not a prophet announcing deliverance but the deliverer in person, and the rejection He meets will take Him to the cross. John says of Him, 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. The type falls short because none of the earlier prophets bore the sin of the people who refused them.

typology.type: The staff and sandals of the Passover traveller
typology.fulfillment: At the first Passover Israel ate 'with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand,' Exodus 12:11, dressed for a journey out of slavery. The Twelve are sent with exactly a staff and sandals, a detail Mark alone gives, and they go out as people on the move, carried by God's provision. Whether Mark intends the Exodus to be heard is not said, so this is an echo and not a declared type. If it is meant, the escalation is that this journey is not out of Egypt but into the world, to proclaim that the greater exodus has begun, as the prophets promised in Isaiah 52:11-12.

typology.type: John as Elijah, Herod and Herodias as Ahab and Jezebel
typology.fulfillment: John comes dressed like Elijah, Mark 1:6, and Jesus later says that Elijah has come and that they did to him whatever they wished, Mark 9:13. The pattern of a wild prophet, a weak king and a vengeful queen is Elijah's own: Ahab was swayed, and Jezebel swore to take Elijah's life, 1 Kings 19:1-2. The type escalates because Elijah escaped into the wilderness and was taken up in a whirlwind, 2 Kings 2:11, while John was killed. He is the forerunner who goes first in suffering as in preaching, and he prepares the way for the One who will go to the cross.

Mark follows the story of the king's birthday feast directly with the story of the feeding of the five thousand, 6:30-44. At the first, nobles feast while a prophet's head is brought on a platter; at the second, a crowd 'like sheep without a shepherd' is seated on the green grass and fed. The contrast shows two kinds of kingship. The first seeks its own honour and pays with a life; the second gives its own life to feed others. The pattern is completed at the Last Supper, 14:22-24, where Jesus gives His body and blood. The comparison is a literary one that Mark invites by his arrangement, not a type that he states.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by three links, and the first is the shape of His rejection. At Nazareth we see in small what will happen on a large scale: the people who think they know Him cannot see Him. They are right about the facts. He is the carpenter, the son of Mary, with brothers and sisters, and yet they miss what matters. The Gospel of John states it from above: 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. And Jesus Himself accepts this place among the prophets. He does not complain but takes up the proverb and goes on teaching from village to village. The Messiah's way is the way of the rejected prophet, and Mark prepares his readers for what happens in Jerusalem.

The second link is the mission. The Twelve are sent in His name with His authority, and what they preach, repentance, is what He preached. The extension of His ministry through them is a picture of how His reign spreads, not by a single great display but through sent ones who depend on Him. He is the Lord who can commission others to do what only God does, to cast out unclean spirits, and so Mark's claim about His identity is repeated through the disciples' work.

The third and strongest link is John's death as a pattern of His own. The forerunner is arrested, bound and killed by a ruler who knows he is righteous but yields to pressure. Pilate will do the same, knowing that Jesus is innocent and handing Him over to please the crowd, Mark 15:10 and 15:15. Both are 'seized' and 'handed over.' Both are killed after a form of trial or whim, and both are buried by followers who take the body and lay it in a tomb. The same unusual word for the corpse appears for both, 6:29 and 15:45. The earlier story prepares the way for the later, and the fate of the forerunner points forward to the fate of the one he announced.

Jesus also fulfils what Herod's banquet lacks. The king's feast is a place of fear, pride and death. Jesus' feast, which Mark sets next to it, is a place of compassion, provision and life. The grief of the king, perilypos, is the word for Jesus' own grief in Gethsemane, and the contrast is plain: the king gives an order he does not want to give because he cannot bear to lose face, while Jesus goes to the cross because He has chosen to bear what His people cannot.

Take care not to over-read. Nazareth's offence at the carpenter is not a code for Jesus' trade, and the platter, the oath and the dancing girl are not coded pictures. The links above are the ones Mark's own arrangement and wording make: the rejected prophet, the sent messengers who carry His authority, and the forerunner whose death anticipates His.

And there is a promise inside the sorrow. When Herod fears that Jesus is John risen from the dead, he is wrong about who Jesus is, but not about what is coming. Resurrection is in the air. The One who is rejected and killed will be the One who is raised, and in that raising the rejection of Nazareth and the death of John are answered.
study.god:
This passage presents a God who works through weakness. He sends a rejected prophet to a village that cannot see Him. He sends twelve men with a staff and sandals to confront the powers of the age. He allows the greatest of the prophets to be killed in a prison by a drunken king's oath. Nothing in the passage suggests that God's purpose depends on these people being welcomed or kept safe. Paul states the same principle later: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, 1 Corinthians 1:27. The Lord of history is not helpless when the faithful are killed, but He lets them be killed, and the story goes on.

He is a God who honours those who speak for Him even when it costs everything. John is called 'righteous and holy,' and the narrator gives no hint that his stand was a mistake. Hebrews 11:38 says of those who suffered that 'the world was not worthy of them.' Heaven's judgment of John is not to be read from the outcome of his trial. This is a hard but needed lesson in how the world's measure of success differs from God's.

He is a God who holds human beings responsible for what they do with truth. Herod heard John gladly and was perplexed and protected him, and still he gave the order. Nothing excuses him. The oath, the guests and the girl's request are the pressures that Mark lists, and the man is still responsible. At the same time, the passage keeps the sovereignty of God over the whole scene in view, since John's death serves the pattern that leads to the cross. The Bible regularly holds both truths without letting either cancel the other, as Peter does in Acts 2:23, where Jesus was handed over 'by God's set purpose and foreknowledge' and put to death 'by the hands of the lawless.'

He is a God who is patient with unbelief and yet takes it seriously. At Nazareth Jesus does not give up on the village; He heals a few and goes on teaching. But the text also says that unbelief limits what is done among them. God does not force His kindness on those who despise it. Every hearer is meant to feel the weight of that.

He is a God who sends. The Lord Jesus gives authority to the Twelve, and the mission is His, not theirs. The ground of the mission is not their ability but the authority given. This hints at the doctrine of the Trinity as it comes to expression elsewhere: the Father sends the Son, and the Son sends His apostles, John 20:21.

For worship, the passage invites praise to a God who is faithful when His servants are not honoured, who uses small and hidden beginnings, and who vindicates His witnesses beyond death. It calls us to the reverence of those who know that the word of God is not ours to edit, as Herod tried to do, but ours to receive, and to the humility of those who see the Lord in the familiar, as Nazareth did not.

crossReferences.note: Joseph's brothers mock him as 'that dreamer' and plot to kill him. The first deliverer of Israel's story is rejected by his own family, and Nazareth's treatment of Jesus in Mark 6:1-6 repeats the pattern, with the difference that Jesus is the greater Deliverer.

God warns Jeremiah that even his brothers and his father's household have betrayed him. The proverb in Mark 6:4 about a prophet without honour among relatives and household has a long history in Israel's experience of her prophets.

Israel ate the Passover dressed for travel, with sandals on their feet and a staff in hand. The Twelve in Mark 6:8-9 are allowed just a staff and sandals, so that the mission has the look of a journey of faith that depends on the LORD's provision.

A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. Sending the Twelve two by two in Mark 6:7 fits this standard of witness, so that the message they carry would be confirmed by more than one voice.

On the night of His arrest Jesus recalls the sending of the Twelve without purse or bag, asks if they lacked anything, and then tells them to take a purse and bag. It shows that the mission rules of Mark 6 were suited to that time and that dependence on God continues.

The law forbids sexual relations with a brother's wife. John's protest, 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife,' Mark 6:18, appeals to this command. He speaks from the law that Herod, as a Jewish ruler, should have kept.

Jezebel sends a message that she will make Elijah's life like the lives of the prophets he had killed. Herodias plays the same part against John, and Mark's Herod, like Ahab, is a king who is drawn to the prophet and yet is led by a stronger will.

The king offers Esther 'even up to half the kingdom.' Herod's oath in Mark 6:23 uses the same extravagant phrase, but in Esther it leads to the saving of a people, while in Mark it leads to the death of a prophet. The echo shows how the same words can serve opposite ends.

God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD. The people's guesses in Mark 6:15 that Jesus is Elijah arise from this hope, and Jesus will say in Mark 9:13 that Elijah has come, meaning John.

Jesus says that Elijah has come and that they did to him whatever they wished. This is the interpretation of John's death that Mark 6 narrates. It shows that the forerunner's suffering was foreseen in Scripture and anticipates the suffering of the Son of Man.

The writer lists faithful people who endured mocking, flogging, chains and the sword, and says the world was not worthy of them. John the Baptist, killed in a prison, belongs to this company, and the passage gives a heavenly verdict on a death that Mark leaves without comment.

'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.' John states the theme of Mark 6:1-6 in a sentence. Nazareth is the first picture in Mark of what the whole nation will do, and the Gospel of John names it as the nature of the rejection.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is the story of a God who keeps sending messengers to a people who keep refusing them. The prophets were stoned, mocked and imprisoned, and Jesus tells a parable about it at the end of His ministry, Mark 12:1-8, where the vineyard owner sends servants and finally his son. Mark 6 is an early chapter of that story. A prophet is dishonoured in his hometown, the Twelve are sent as His heralds, and the forerunner is killed. Each scene belongs to the long history of God's word meeting resistance.

The chapter shows that the kingdom does not advance by worldly power. Herod has all the power in the scene. He has the soldiers, the guests and the prison, and yet the story is about the weakness of power: a king who cannot do the right thing because of what others might think. The word of God goes forward in a different way, through the poor travellers who are sent with a staff. This answers a question the whole Bible raises, how God's purposes can come to pass in a world ruled by people like Herod. They come through the faithfulness of witnesses, even to death, and in a way that no ruler's power can prevent.

It also points back to Eden and forward to the cross. The sin of the garden was a refusal to listen to God's word, and Nazareth and Herod repeat it in two ways: one in contemptuous familiarity, the other in listening that does not obey. The need is for a hearing that bears fruit, as in the good soil of chapter 4. And it points forward, since John's death is a sign of what the world will do with the One he announced. The cross is where the rejection reaches its height and where God turns it into redemption, as Peter says in Acts 2:23-24 and Joseph said of his brothers' crime, 'God intended it for good,' Genesis 50:20.

The story does not end with the platter and the prison. Mark's next scene is the feeding in the wilderness, where the true King gives life to the hungry. The messengers who were rejected, the prophets who were killed and John who lost his head are not forgotten. Hebrews says the world was not worthy of them, and Revelation sees under the altar the souls of those who were slain for the word of God and sees them given white robes, Revelation 6:9-11. In the new creation the messengers are vindicated and honoured. The prophet without honour at home is the King on the throne, and those who followed Him in dishonour share His glory, Romans 8:17. The household that did not believe becomes a household of every nation, and the table that Herod's guests spoiled is replaced by the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.

quiz.q: Why did the people of Nazareth take offense at Jesus?

options.text: Their familiarity with Him as the local carpenter tripped them into unbelief, despite His evident wisdom and miracles.
options.note: Mark 6:3-6; they could not see past His ordinary origins and stumbled into unbelief.

options.text: Because His teaching was too hard to understand.
options.note: They were astonished at His wisdom; the problem was not comprehension but offense at His familiar background.

options.text: Because He performed no miracles among them at all.
options.note: He did heal a few; their unbelief came first and limited the works, rather than the reverse.

options.text: Because He claimed not to be from Nazareth.
options.note: They knew Him as a local; His origins were the very cause of their offense.

quiz.q: How did Jesus send out the Twelve?

options.text: Two by two, with His authority over demons but almost no provisions, dependent on Him and on others' hospitality.
options.note: Mark 6:7-9; they took a staff only, relying on God and hosts.

options.text: Two by two to preach and heal in the towns.
options.note: Correct as far as it goes, but it omits the striking vulnerability and dependence of taking nothing.

options.text: Alone, each to a different distant nation.
options.note: They went two by two in nearby towns, not singly to distant nations.

options.text: With ample supplies and money for a long journey.
options.note: The opposite; He told them to take nothing but a staff.

quiz.q: What message did the Twelve preach?

options.text: That people should repent, the same call Jesus and John proclaimed.
options.note: Mark 6:12; they preached repentance.

options.text: That people should be healed and freed from demons.
options.note: They did heal and cast out demons, but their preached message was the call to repent.

options.text: That the Twelve themselves should be honoured.
options.note: They went in humble dependence, pointing to the kingdom, not to themselves.

options.text: That the law of Moses was now abolished.
options.note: Their message was repentance in view of the kingdom, not the abolition of the law.

quiz.q: Why did Herod have John the Baptist beheaded?

options.text: Pride and human respect: a rash oath before his guests, exploited by Herodias, overrode his own fear and regard for John.
options.note: Mark 6:26-27; Herod acted to save face despite knowing John was righteous.

options.text: Because John had rebuked his unlawful marriage to Herodias.
options.note: That was the underlying grievance, but the immediate cause was Herod's oath and fear of his guests.

options.text: Because John had plotted against Herod's throne.
options.note: John had not plotted; he had spoken the truth about Herod's marriage.

options.text: Because Herod had never respected John.
options.note: Herod feared and protected John and listened to him gladly, which makes the murder more tragic.

quiz.q: What does Herod's example warn us about?

options.text: That one can hear the truth gladly and even admire the messenger, yet refuse to repent and obey.
options.note: Herod listened gladly but would not turn, and pride finally silenced the voice he respected.

options.text: That powerful people often dislike prophets.
options.note: True in general, but Herod actually liked John; the sharper warning is admiring truth without obeying it.

options.text: That making promises is always sinful.
options.note: The issue was a rash, sinful oath kept out of pride, not the making of promises as such.

options.text: That God's messengers are always protected from harm.
options.note: John was martyred; faithful witness can cost one's life.

questions: The people of Nazareth missed Jesus because they thought they already knew Him. Where might overfamiliarity be dulling your wonder at who Jesus is?
The Twelve were sent out in radical dependence on God and others. What would it look like for you to serve God with less self-reliance and more trust?
John spoke the truth to a powerful man even at great cost. Where is God calling you to speak or live the truth when it would be safer to stay silent?
Herod listened to John gladly but would not repent. Is there truth you enjoy hearing but have not yet obeyed?
John's faithfulness led to a martyr's death, yet he prepared the way for the Saviour. How does John's example shape your view of a life measured by faithfulness rather than by comfort or success?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts read he was saying rather than people were saying; either way the report circulated that John had risen, which pricked Herod's guilty conscience.
Some early manuscripts read his daughter Herodias rather than the daughter of Herodias; the girl is the daughter of Herodias in either case, and the account is unaffected.
